pages.why: A private credit fund, which lends directly to companies, is weighing a loan to a restaurant chain whose profits have risen for three years. Its analyst turns straight to the cash flow statement, because loans are repaid in cash, not profit. It shows the chain spending more cash on new outlets than its restaurants bring in.
pages.idea:
The **cash flow statement** shows the cash that came in and went out over a period. It sorts every movement into three sections, which add up to the change in cash:

- **Cash from operations**: cash from running the business, such as cash in from customers and cash out to staff, suppliers and landlords.
- **Cash from investing**: cash spent on or received from long-term assets. The main item is usually **capital expenditure**, or capex: spending on assets that last for years, such as new cafés and ovens.
- **Cash from financing**: cash to and from lenders and shareholders, such as new loans, loan repayments, selling new shares and paying dividends.

Most companies build cash from operations by the indirect method: they start from profit, add back costs that used no cash that year, mainly depreciation, then adjust for cash tied up in the business. When receivables or inventory grow, cash is held back. When payables grow, suppliers are funding the business, which keeps cash in.

**Free cash flow** is cash from operations minus capital expenditure: the cash left after keeping and growing the business, which can repay debt or go to shareholders. Firms define it differently, so always ask which one is meant.

Profitable companies can still run out of cash. A fast-growing chain pays for new cafés before they earn anything, and slow-paying corporate customers tie up more cash in receivables. Profit can rise every year while cash drains away.

example.text:
Brew Lane's FY26 cash flow statement, simplified: interest and tax stay inside cash from operations. Real statements have many more lines, and Indian ones usually show interest paid under financing.

{table}

Operations: profit of 9, plus 5 of depreciation, which used no cash. Receivables and inventory each grew by 1, tying up cash, while payables grew by 1, keeping cash in: 9 + 5 − 1 − 1 + 1 = 13.

Investing: 10 of capital expenditure. Financing: 1 of the bank loan repaid, no dividend.

Net change: 13 − 10 − 1 = 2, so cash rose from 6 to 8, matching the 31 March 2026 balance sheet.

Free cash flow is 13 − 10 = ₹3 crore. Most of the cash it generated went straight back into new assets.

terms.definition: Cash coming in and going out over a period, sorted into operating, investing and financing sections.
terms.formula: Opening cash + operating + investing + financing = closing cash

terms.definition: Cash generated by running the business: profit, adjusted for costs that used no cash and for changes in receivables, inventory and payables.
Cash spent on or received from long-term assets and investments, such as capex, buying a business or selling property.

aka: purchase of property, plant and equipment
terms.definition: Spending on assets that last more than a year, such as cafés and ovens. Their cost reaches profit slowly, as depreciation.
Cash to and from lenders and shareholders: new borrowing, loan repayments, money raised by selling new shares, and dividends.
Cash left after running and investing in the business, free to repay debt or reward shareholders. Definitions vary, so state which one is used.

pages.builder:
After the balance sheet equation, the cash flow statement gives you a second free check: closing cash must equal cash on the balance sheet at the same date. Real differences, such as an overdraft counted as negative cash, are reconciled in a note. Otherwise a failure means a misread line or a lost sign: brackets mark outflows, and an extractor that drops them turns an outflow into an inflow.

Free cash flow raises a different problem. One client means cash from operations minus capex; another also takes off interest, lease payments or dividends. So never store the bare number. Store its definition and inputs with it: FCF 3 = cash from operations 13 − capex 10.

**Check worth building:** for every period, test that closing cash equals balance sheet cash, and flag any gap with both figures.

client.say: Free cash flow is defined differently from firm to firm, so I'd like to match your team's definition before we calculate anything.
client.ask: Which free cash flow definition does your team use?

quiz.prompt: A café chain's profit has risen for three years, yet its cash keeps falling. Which explanation fits best?
options: Its profit must be overstated, since profit always turns into cash
Its share price has fallen, which reduces the cash it holds
It is opening cafés fast, and its customers are paying more slowly
Its depreciation is rising, and depreciation is paid out in cash
quiz.explain: Growth uses cash before it earns any: new cafés need capital expenditure, and slower payers tie up cash in receivables, while profit keeps rising. Overstated profit is the tempting answer, but profit and cash routinely differ, so the gap alone does not prove an error.

quiz.prompt: When Brew Lane builds its cash from operations, why does it add its ₹5 crore of depreciation back to profit?
options: Depreciation cut profit, but no cash left the business for it
Depreciation is a source of cash that the business can spend
Depreciation is refunded by the tax authority at the end of the year
Depreciation belongs in investing, so it moves to that section
quiz.explain: Depreciation spreads the cost of equipment bought earlier, so it lowers profit though no cash leaves in FY26; the cash left at purchase, as capital expenditure. Calling it a source of cash is the tempting mistake: adding it back only undoes a cost that used no cash.

quiz.prompt: Brew Lane's FY26 profit after tax is ₹9 crore and its depreciation ₹5 crore. During the year, receivables rose by ₹1 crore, inventory by ₹1 crore and payables by ₹1 crore. What is its cash from operations?
quiz.explain: 9 + 5 − 1 − 1 + 1 = ₹13 crore: more receivables and inventory tie up cash, while more unpaid supplier bills keep cash in the business. 11 is the common slip, from treating the rise in payables as a use of cash.

quiz.prompt: Brew Lane's FY26 cash from operations is ₹13 crore, its capital expenditure ₹10 crore and its debt repaid ₹1 crore. Using cash from operations minus capital expenditure, what is its free cash flow?
options: ₹2 crore
₹3 crore
₹9 crore
₹23 crore
quiz.explain: Free cash flow is 13 − 10 = ₹3 crore, the cash left after investing in the business. ₹2 crore is tempting, but it also takes off the loan repayment, which this definition leaves out, and so gives the change in cash instead.

quiz.prompt: An analyst at an investment fund says, 'Can you pull free cash flow for these 30 companies?' Which reply is best?
options: Sure, we will copy the free cash flow figure each company reports.
Shall we send EBITDA instead? It is very close to free cash flow.
We would rather not, as free cash flow is not an audited figure.
Happy to. Is that operations minus capex, or after interest too?
quiz.explain: Free cash flow has several definitions, so agreeing on one before pulling 30 companies makes your numbers match the client's. Copying each company's reported figure is tempting, but many do not report one, and those that do define it their own way.

quiz.concept: Tie closing cash to balance sheet
quiz.prompt: Your system reads Brew Lane's FY26 cash flow statement as: opening cash 6, operations 13, investing 10, financing (1). It then reports closing cash of ₹28 crore. Which check would have caught the error?
options: Recompute closing cash as opening cash plus the three sections
Check that cash from operations is larger than profit after tax
Compare closing cash with the ₹8 crore on the balance sheet
Confirm that the statement covers the year to 31 March 2026
quiz.explain: The balance sheet shows ₹8 crore of cash at 31 March 2026, so 28 fails at once; the cause is the investing outflow of (10) read as +10. Recomputing from the three sections is the trap: it repeats the sign error and agrees with 28.

speak.prompt: In 30 seconds, tell a client why a profitable company can still run out of cash.
speak.modelAnswer: Profit and cash are measured differently. Profit counts a sale when it's made, even if the customer pays later, and it spreads the cost of equipment over many years. Cash only counts money that actually moved. A growing company pays for new sites before they earn anything, and unpaid customer bills pile up. Brew Lane made ₹9 crore of profit in FY26 but only ₹3 crore of free cash flow, mainly because it spent ₹10 crore on new assets. Loans are repaid from cash, not profit.
